A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multifidelity inference work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained algorithms and experiments across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation experiments on the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, a multicompartmental neuron, and a recurrent spiking network, including posterior accuracy, calibration, and predictive checks.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and adds SLCP, SIR, and image experiments, controlled transfer-learning analyses, baseline comparisons, and computational-cost measurements.

M1.justification: The original MF-NPE, MF-TSNPE, and acquisition-based algorithms retain their objectives and core procedures. V3 adds an explicit extension that transfers weights through multiple fidelity levels (Appendix L) and a CNN-embedding adaptation for image observations (Appendix E.6). These are limited extensions of the existing approach.

E1.justification: V3 retains all three original tasks and adds SLCP parameter inference, epidemiological SIR inference, and Gaussian Blob image inference using different image resolutions across fidelities. These substantially expand the represented domains, posterior structures, and observation types. Appendix B additionally evaluates noisy and coordinate-reversed OU observations.

E2.justification: V3 adds standalone TSNPE to the OU comparison (Figure 2) and MF-ABC to OU2, OU3, and OU4 (Figure 8), where v1 Figure 3 uses NPE as the baseline. MF-ABC was previously cited but not evaluated. Sequential multifidelity methods also enter the neuron comparisons in Figures 3B and 13.

E3.justification: V3 adds MMD and NRMSE evaluations, importance-resampling reference posteriors for SLCP/SIR, image preprocessing, and controlled perturbation protocols. It introduces per-observation sequential neuron evaluation and revises reported evaluation sizes. For example, spiking-network evaluation uses 1,000 observations in v1 Figure 5, versus 10,000 in v3 Figure 3, while v3 Appendix D.1 states 262,008. These documented changes and inconsistencies preclude exact matched-setting comparisons for affected results.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained pretraining-budget, parameter-dimensionality, calibration, and predictive analyses, v3 adds controlled noise/representation perturbations (Appendix B), MF-ABC threshold sensitivity and posterior diagnostics (F.1.1), joint low/high-fidelity pretraining experiments (H.3), posterior-distance analysis (J), and simulation-versus-training cost analysis (K). These directly investigate transfer effectiveness, alternative initialization, baseline sensitivity, and practical efficiency.

E5.justification: Ten-initialization averages and 95% confidence intervals already appear in v1. V3 adds explicit single-initialization reporting for costly non-amortized evaluations, mean and standard deviation for posterior distances (Table 3), and five-run timing summaries with standard deviations for L5PC (Table 4). This expands statistical documentation without establishing increased replication of the original experiments.

E6.justification: V3 adds benchmark accuracy curves, sequential neuron results, posterior-distance measurements, and computational-cost tables. It newly reports little acquisition benefit on SLCP/SIR and no clear advantage from joint pretraining. The reported neuron high/low-fidelity simulation-time ratio changes from approximately seven to four, without establishing matched hardware conditions. Conversely, the original firing-rate fractions of 66.4%, 94.2%, and 95.6% are retained in Figure 3F.

T1.justification: V3 Appendix C adds an explicit large-sample derivation connecting the NPE loss to expected posterior KL divergence, whereas v1 states related properties without this derivation. Appendix B adds mathematical definitions for controlled perturbations and information-invariance reasoning. These are limited formal additions; they do not establish a new transfer-learning convergence-rate guarantee.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain low-to-high-fidelity transfer learning and two sequential schemes, with the retained claim of up to two orders of magnitude fewer high-fidelity simulations. V3's introduction extends the explicit efficiency claim from comparison with NPE to comparison with both NPE and TSNPE. Its more prominent naming of the sequential variants does not constitute a new original contribution.

C2.justification: V1 discusses shared features, simulator similarity, dimensionality, and ensemble overhead. V3 substantially develops this interpretation: Section 4.4 and Appendices B/J distinguish shared information from representational coherence and argue that posterior distance alone does not predict transfer success. Appendix K grounds the existing ensemble-cost caveat in measured tradeoffs, while the discussion adds guidance about when acquisition is worthwhile and the unresolved allocation of budgets across fidelities.

D1.justification: V3 expands v1's basic architecture and preprocessing description with software versions/licenses, Adam optimization, batch size 200, learning rate 0.0005, validation fraction, stopping patience, hardware, parallelization, and measured training costs (Appendices D/G/K). Appendix F.1.1 documents the MF-ABC implementation and settings. Section 6 promises code and data release upon publication; it does not establish present availability.

R1.justification: V3 replaces the model-misspecification/ROPE discussion with substantially expanded positioning around simulation-efficient SBI, surrogate approaches, and concurrent multifidelity work by Thiele, Hikida, and Saoulis and colleagues. It also adds transfer-learning theory references and qualifies the earlier statement that transfer learning's potential for SBI had not been realized. These changes materially update the research context.

P1.justification: V3 reorganizes the results around a general benchmarking section, moves the detailed OU exposition into appendices, replaces the related-work subsection structure with thematic Background paragraphs, and extensively reorganizes the supplementary material. The abstract and method exposition are revised, acquisition-bias discussion moves to Appendix M, and reproducibility, acknowledgments, and LLM-use statements are added. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V3 changes the main text from two columns to one, redraws the method schematic with neuron examples, and rebuilds the benchmark plots with additional metric panels. Original neuroscience figures and the firing-rate table are combined into Figure 3, while posterior and predictive displays move into appendices. New perturbation, image, sensitivity, posterior-distance, and cost displays constitute substantial visual redesign beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the efficiency claims. Evaluated TSNPE and MF-ABC comparisons address important comparator gaps in v1, while distinct benchmarks, controlled transfer analyses, and total-cost accounting make generality and practical efficiency more assessable. Expanded implementation details further improve reproducibility. Conflicting evaluation counts in Figure 3 and Appendix D.1 remain a material weakness, and code release is still deferred, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and explanation.
